segments.text: Okay everyone, settle down. Today we start halogenoalkanes, chapter sixteen in the coursebook.
A halogenoalkane is simply an alkane where one or more hydrogen atoms have been replaced by a halogen atom.
So we classify them as primary halogenoalkane, secondary halogenoalkane or tertiary halogenoalkane depending on the carbon bearing the halogen.
Primary means the carbon attached to the halogen has one other carbon attached to it. Tertiary means three.
Now the key reaction for this chapter is nucleophilic substitution. Write that down, it comes up every single year.
The carbon halogen bond is polar because the halogen is more electronegative, so the carbon carries a partial positive charge.
That partial positive carbon is what attracts a nucleophile. A nucleophile is an electron pair donor, it seeks a positive centre.
Common nucleophiles for us are the hydroxide ion, the cyanide ion, and ammonia. Learn those three.
With hydroxide you get hydrolysis, and the product is an alcohol. With cyanide you get a nitrile, and importantly you extend the carbon chain by one.
Now there are two mechanisms for nucleophilic substitution and you need both. They are called SN1 and SN2.
SN2 is a one step mechanism. The nucleophile attacks at the same time as the leaving group departs. Draw the curly arrows carefully.
SN2 is favoured by primary halogenoalkanes because there is less steric hindrance around that carbon.
SN1 is a two step mechanism. First the carbon halogen bond breaks heterolytically to form a carbocation intermediate.
Then the nucleophile attacks that carbocation. SN1 is favoured by tertiary halogenoalkanes because the tertiary carbocation is more stable.
Why is it more stable? Because the alkyl groups push electron density towards the positive centre. That is the inductive effect.
Secondary halogenoalkanes sit in between and can go by either mechanism, so do not be surprised to see both.
Right, now let us look at how the rate of hydrolysis depends on which halogen is present.
We test this with silver nitrate solution in ethanol. The halide ion released forms a silver halide precipitate.
The iodo compound reacts fastest and gives a yellow precipitate of silver iodide. The chloro compound is slowest, white precipitate.
And the reason is bond enthalpy. The carbon iodine bond is the weakest, so it breaks most easily. Carbon fluorine is the strongest.
That is a really common exam question, so make sure you say bond enthalpy and not electronegativity. Electronegativity is the wrong answer there.
Last thing for today. As well as substitution, halogenoalkanes undergo elimination reactions.
If you use hydroxide in hot ethanol rather than in aqueous solution, the hydroxide acts as a base and you get elimination.
The product is an alkene, plus water, plus the halide ion. Same reagent, different conditions, completely different product.
So aqueous conditions give substitution and an alcohol. Ethanolic conditions give elimination and an alkene. That distinction is worth marks.
Finally, a word on the environment. Chlorofluorocarbons are halogenoalkanes and they damage the ozone layer.
Ultraviolet light breaks the carbon chlorine bond homolytically, producing chlorine free radicals which then catalyse ozone breakdown.
Right, that is the chapter. Do the nucleophilic substitution mechanism questions for Thursday and draw every curly arrow.
